summary: Lists the hosts that provide any of the small TCP utility services, based on tests run in February and March 1983. It is a survey report, not a specification.

eli5.summary: A list of computers that offer tiny extra services, like echoing back what you say.

questions: which hosts offer small tcp services
subtitle: A survey listing which Internet hosts offered small TCP utility services like Echo, Discard, and Finger.

tldr.problem: It was unclear which hosts on the early Internet actually implemented the small 'utility' TCP services designed for testing and administration.
tldr.mechanism: This survey tests nine well-known TCP services on hosts listed in the NIC host table of 24 February 1983: Echo (port 7), Discard (9), Active Users/systat (11), Date and Time (13), Netstat (15), Quote of the Day (17), Character Generator (19), Finger (79), and Time (37). Results are reported by service and by host.
tldr.outcome: The survey shows deployment varied widely by service. Time (port 37) was most common with 60 hosts, while Active Users and Quote of the Day appeared on roughly 15-16 hosts each. This RFC is not a specification but a survey report.

today: RFC 848 is a historic survey report. These utility services are documented in the TCP standards but are rarely enabled or used on modern hosts due to security concerns and the availability of more modern diagnostic tools.

sections.title: The Little TCP Services
sections.content:
RFC 848 surveys which hosts provide nine small TCP utility services defined in the early Internet standards. These services are simple, quick to test, and useful for network diagnosis and configuration. The services range from trivial (Echo simply echoes back what it receives) to informational (Finger shows logged-in users).

The nine services tested are: Echo (port 7), Discard (port 9), Active Users or systat (port 11), Date and Time in printable form (port 13), Netstat (port 15), Quote of the Day (port 17), Character Generator or ttytst (port 19), Finger (port 79), and a 32-bit binary Time service (port 37). The test period was 23-24 February and 3-5 March 1983, run from ISI-VAXA.ARPA against hosts in the NIC hostname table.
sections.eli5: There are nine tiny programs that live on some computers. One repeats what you say, one throws away messages, one tells the time, one tells jokes—this survey says which computers run which ones.

sections.title: Which Hosts Offered Which Services
sections.content:
The survey results show significant variation in service deployment. The Time service (port 37) was most widely implemented, with 60 hosts offering it. Echo appeared on 38 hosts, Discard on 29, Finger on 35, and Netstat on 21. Quote of the Day appeared on 16 hosts, Character Generator on 19, and Active Users on only 7. Date and Time (port 13) was offered by 15 hosts.

The results are presented in two formats: first grouped by service with lists of participating hosts, and then as a summary showing that different host types and network regions had different levels of service support. This snapshot shows how quickly and unevenly these small services were adopted across the early Internet.
sections.eli5: The survey found 60 different computers saying the time, 38 echoing back, 35 showing who is logged in with Finger, and so on. Not every computer offers every service.

sections.title: Service Deployment Summary
sections.content: The wide variation in service support reflects the early stage of Internet standardization. Some services like Time and Echo were nearly universal, while others like Active Users saw adoption on only a handful of hosts. This variation tells the story of the early Internet, where implementers chose which services to support based on their own needs.
sections.eli5: Different computers offered different services. This shows that people were still figuring out which services were useful.
